tips: An argument about whether a cost is worth paying needs the difference between two conditions, not a single figure.

whyCorrect: The conclusion is that a maker should hold the cave near the top of the humidity range, so the support has to show that the top of the range keeps the most moisture in. At 95% humidity the wheels lost 3.1% of their mass against 11.4% at 80%, less than a third as much, which is the case for choosing the highest humidity tested.

whyWrong.A: The middle result confirms the trend but is not the value the team recommends and offers no comparison in itself.
whyWrong.B: The largest loss at 80% shows the low end is bad without showing what the high end achieves.
whyWrong.C: The spread of humidities describes the design of the experiment, not what the results show.

commonMistakes: Citing whichever row is most extreme in loss. A recommendation for one end of a range needs that end's figure set against the other.

whyCorrect: The curer's fish sits at 0.83, so any organism needing more than 0.83 is blocked and any organism that grows below it is not. Clostridium botulinum needs 0.94 and Staphylococcus aureus 0.86, both above 0.83, and those are the two bacteria that cause acute illness; the yeasts at 0.80 and the xerophilic moulds at 0.61 can still grow, which is the spoilage the curer concedes. That split is exactly the argument.

whyWrong.A: Botulinum alone leaves out Staphylococcus, so it cannot support a claim about every illness-causing organism on the list.
whyWrong.B: The overall range of the table says nothing about where 0.83 falls within it.
whyWrong.D: The moulds are the organisms the curer admits are not excluded, so this supports the concession rather than the safety claim.

tips: With a threshold argument, sort the table into rows above and rows below the stated value before reading the choices.

whyCorrect: The text rules out the winter explanation in its second sentence: with the door shut, the surrounding earth governs everything, so aspect is irrelevant then. The threat it does identify belongs to the shoulder seasons, when the door is opened daily and a low sun would send light and warm air into a south-facing doorway. So the orientation guards the store during the times it is opened, not during the coldest weather.

whyWrong.B: The passage says the earth governs the chamber in winter and the door is shut, which is the reason winter is not the answer.
whyWrong.C: Darkness is never discussed, and a low sun reaching the doorway is a daytime effect.
whyWrong.D: A high summer sun is precisely when a doorway is not reached, so summer is not the season being defended against.

commonMistakes: Assuming a cellar is designed against the coldest weather. The text names the opposite threat, warmth entering through an open door.

whyCorrect: The passage says pond ice could still undercut mechanical ice on price and that the harvesters were untroubled by it. What killed the trade was that a plant could be built wherever ice was wanted, while pond ice had to be cut in one place, stored through a summer and carried hundreds of miles. Once plants were everywhere the buyer no longer needed anything carried, so the distance that had made the harvesters' service worth paying for simply vanished.

whyWrong.B: The passage says harvesters kept a price advantage, so cost was not where they lost.
whyWrong.C: No buyer reluctance is mentioned; the plants spread and were used.
whyWrong.D: Ice quality is never raised anywhere in the text.

tips: The words "less on price than on" tell you to look for the non-price factor the passage has already named.

whyCorrect: Everything up to the blank is a subordinate clause opening with "When" and containing two verbs, drew and found. It cannot stand alone, so the main clause "he was looking at a class of molecule" must follow it after a comma. An introductory subordinate clause takes a comma before the main clause.

whyWrong.A: With no punctuation, "explain he was looking" runs together and the reader loses the boundary of the When clause.
whyWrong.B: A semicolon requires an independent clause on both sides, and a When clause is not one.
whyWrong.C: A colon likewise needs a complete sentence before it.

tips: Sentences that open with When, If, Because or Although reach their main clause after a comma, never a semicolon.

whyCorrect: Everything before the blank is a complete sentence ending in the participial phrase "leaving the pyloric caeca in place." What follows is not another independent clause but an explanation of that choice, so a colon is the mark that fits: it needs a full sentence in front of it and introduces the elaboration behind it. The comma after "deliberately" then sets off the reason clause beginning with "since."

whyWrong.A: A semicolon must have an independent clause on both sides, and "deliberately, since they carry the digestive enzymes" has no subject or main verb of its own.
whyWrong.B: A comma is too weak to introduce the explanation, and running "deliberately since" together loses the pause that separates the comment from its reason.
whyWrong.C: With no punctuation at all, "in place deliberately since" runs the statement and its explanation into one undifferentiated string.

tips: A colon needs a complete sentence before it but not after it, which is why it can introduce a phrase a semicolon cannot.

whyCorrect: "The tool that did the real work on a frozen pond was not the saw but the ice plough" is a complete sentence. The words after the blank form a second one, in which "A heavy toothed blade set in a wooden frame and dragged behind a horse" is a descriptive phrase attached to the subject of "it cut a groove." Ending the first sentence with a full stop and beginning the second with that phrase punctuates both correctly.

whyWrong.A: Without punctuation, "the ice plough a heavy toothed blade" runs two noun phrases together with nothing to mark the break.
whyWrong.B: A semicolon here makes the long descriptive phrase look like a continuation of the first sentence, so the reader takes "a heavy toothed blade" as another item after "the saw."
whyWrong.D: A comma after "plough" makes the phrase an appositive, and then "it cut a groove" is spliced onto the same sentence with only a comma.

commonMistakes: Assuming a long trailing phrase must be attached to the previous sentence; here it belongs to the clause that follows it.

whyCorrect: The blank falls in the middle of a single measurement, "four tenths of a degree," which is the complement of "was." Nothing is being joined or set off, so no punctuation belongs there at all.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon would cut the sentence in two and leave "tenths of a degree" standing without a subject or verb.
whyWrong.B: A colon would announce a list or explanation, but "tenths of a degree" simply completes the phrase already begun by "four."
whyWrong.D: A comma separates a number from its own unit, which is never correct.

tips: Before choosing any mark, check whether the words on either side of the blank belong to a single phrase; if they do, the answer is no punctuation.

whyCorrect: The second half of the sentence is a clause of its own, joined by "and," with "the drain" as its subject. That subject is singular and the sentence is in the present tense to match "slopes," so the verb is runs.

whyWrong.A: "Running" is a participle, which would leave the second clause with no finite verb.
whyWrong.B: "To run" is an infinitive and cannot serve as the main verb of the clause.
whyWrong.D: "Run" is the plural form and does not agree with the singular "drain."

tips: When "and" joins two clauses, check the second clause's own subject rather than the one at the start of the sentence.

whyCorrect: The relative clause "it leaves behind" describes the patch, and its subject is "it," standing for the ice. A singular subject in the present tense takes the -s form, and the present matches the general statement made in the rest of the passage.

whyWrong.B: "Leave" is the plural form and does not agree with the singular "it."
whyWrong.C: "Leaving" is a participle, so the relative clause would have no finite verb.
whyWrong.D: "Had left" is past perfect and places the event before some earlier past time, which conflicts with the present-tense description of what freezer burn is.

commonMistakes: Choosing the plural because "patches" appears nearby; the subject of this clause is the singular "it."

whyCorrect: The blank needs a possessive modifying "surfaces," and the owners are "fish that touch one another," which is plural. The plural possessive determiner is their.

whyWrong.B: "Its" is singular and would point back to one fish, not to the fish touching each other.
whyWrong.C: "They're" is the contraction of they are, which cannot modify a noun.
whyWrong.D: "There" is an adverb of place and shows no possession at all.

tips: Read the blank with the noun after it. If the phrase means "belonging to them," only their works.

whyCorrect: The second sentence identifies a problem: a fish straight from the brine is wet, so the smoke droplets dissolve into the film of water and run off. The third gives the practice that answers it, hanging the fish until a tacky pellicle forms. The practice exists because of the problem, so the transition marks cause and effect.

whyWrong.A: "Meanwhile" places two things in the same stretch of time, but drying comes before smoking, not alongside it.
whyWrong.C: "By comparison" needs two things measured against each other; the third sentence gives a remedy, not a comparison.
whyWrong.D: "Admittedly" concedes a point against the argument, and this sentence supports it.

tips: A sentence describing what people do about a problem just stated is a consequence, so look for a because-style transition.

whyCorrect: The second sentence sets an expectation, that a sixtyfold rise in blood glucose would be an emergency in a mammal. The third reports that the frog clears it in days with no detectable damage. The outcome runs against the expectation just raised, so the transition has to be adversative.

whyWrong.B: "Therefore" would make the frog's recovery a consequence of the mammalian emergency, which reverses the logic.
whyWrong.C: "In addition" would add another similar fact, but this fact cuts against the previous one.
whyWrong.D: "That is" introduces a restatement, and the frog's recovery is new information rather than the same point rephrased.

commonMistakes: Missing that the mammal sentence is there only to make the frog's tolerance surprising.

whyCorrect: The second sentence gives the disadvantage of sea water at three per cent, enormous fuel before any yield. The third gives the opposite case, an inland spring at twenty-five per cent worked profitably in a climate where no pond would ever dry. The two sentences set weak brine against strong brine, so the transition marks contrast.

whyWrong.A: "Accordingly" would make the spring's profitability a consequence of sea water being expensive, but it follows from the spring's own strength.
whyWrong.B: "Furthermore" adds a further point on the same side, and this sentence switches to the other side of the comparison.
whyWrong.D: "For instance" would make the spring an example of the sea water claim, which it contradicts.

tips: When two consecutive sentences name two different materials with opposite results, the transition is contrastive.

whyCorrect: The goal has two parts: a low-cost device and a change in the sellers' commercial position rather than only in the crop. Only this choice carries both, the two-dollar cost and the twenty-seven days against three, and then the commercial consequence, that sellers could hold stock until prices rose instead of selling everything at once.

whyWrong.A: The cost alone says nothing about what the device achieved.
whyWrong.B: Naming the comparison sets up the trial without reporting any result.
whyWrong.D: The shelf-life figures describe the condition of the crop, which the goal explicitly says is not enough on its own.

tips: When a goal says "not merely X," strike out every choice that stops at X.

whyCorrect: The goal is what the comparison shows about how the trait arose, so the sentence needs the long separation of the lineages, the structural difference between the molecules, the shared function, and the conclusion that follows. Only this choice supplies all four and states the conclusion, that the trait was reached twice rather than inherited once.

whyWrong.A: The shared mechanism alone is consistent with common inheritance, so it settles nothing about origin.
whyWrong.C: That both groups survive below freezing states the shared trait without any evidence about how it came about.
whyWrong.D: The structural contrast is half the argument; without the long separation and the shared function it does not show independent origin.

commonMistakes: Picking the note about the shared mechanism. Shared function points to convergence only when paired with unrelated structure and separate ancestry.

whyCorrect: The goal asks how a supposed pest contributes to the finished cheese, so the sentence needs the damage the mites do, the physical effect of that damage, and the benefit to the cheese. This choice gives the pitted grey crust, the multiplied surface area letting air and moisture reach the paste, and the flatter, slower-ripening wheels kept free of mites.

whyWrong.A: Naming the mite and where it lives introduces the organism without any contribution.
whyWrong.B: The pitting alone reads as damage, since nothing here says what the pitting achieves.
whyWrong.C: The comparison with mite-free wheels shows there is a benefit but never explains the mechanism behind it.

tips: For a "how it contributes" goal, the answer normally contains both the mechanism and the outcome it produces.

whyCorrect: The passage states a duty the keeper could not avoid, being at the bar before the vehicle, and shows that a square house made it impossible because it left one road unseen. The angled room with a window in each face is the only arrangement that meets the duty. So the shape was forced by the job, which makes it a requirement rather than a style choice.

whyWrong.B: A compromise gives something up on both sides, but the angled room loses nothing; it covers both roads completely.
whyWrong.C: Decoration is what the sentence rules out when it says the shape was not a fashion.
whyWrong.D: Convenience understates it. The keeper could not do his work at all without seeing both approaches.

tips: "Not X but ___" tells you the blank must be the opposite kind of thing from X, here practical necessity against style.

whyCorrect: The problem is a smooth plate sliding on frost, and the fix is a turned-down heel and raised nail heads so that the foot bites instead of sliding. The last sentence trades a small loss in the evenness of the tread against a large gain, and the gain the whole passage has described is traction. That is grip.

whyWrong.A: Comfort works against the description, since a spur and raised nails make the tread less even.
whyWrong.B: Appearance is never mentioned; every detail concerns how the foot holds the road.
whyWrong.D: Speed is not the issue. The additions stop a horse from slipping, and nothing suggests it moves faster.

commonMistakes: Choosing a general benefit like comfort or speed when the passage has named one specific problem the change solves.

whyCorrect: The watch was locked in a case only the offices could open, so the guard could not move the hands either way. The clause before the blank spells out both directions he was prevented from tampering in, which means the record could not be shaped by the men whose performance it measured. A record the crew cannot influence is independent of them.

whyWrong.A: Protective would say the record shielded the crew, but the point is that it could convict them of a late start.
whyWrong.C: Typical is a claim about how ordinary the journey was, and nothing in the passage compares journeys.
whyWrong.D: Critical in the sense of fault-finding attributes an attitude to a sheet of recorded times; the passage stresses only that the crew could not alter it.

tips: When a sentence lists what someone could not do, the blank usually names the resulting freedom from their influence.

whyCorrect: The bidder paid a fixed sum whether the year proved good or bad, and a wet season that kept wagons off the road fell on him rather than on the trust. The sentence is balanced: the trust gets a figure it can count on, and the bidder gets whatever the trust has given up. What the trust has given up is exposure to a bad year, which is risk.

whyWrong.B: Profit is only half the picture and ignores the wet season the passage puts on the bidder's side of the ledger.
whyWrong.C: Labour is not the subject of the sentence, which is about who bears the consequences of a bad season.
whyWrong.D: Authority over the gate comes with the contract, but the balanced structure requires the opposite of the trust's certainty.

commonMistakes: Reading the arrangement only from the winning side. The contrast with the trust's guaranteed figure requires a word about uncertainty.

whyCorrect: The first sentence names the danger: the hoof wears faster than it grows, and a lame beast is worth less at the end of the road. The crescents are nailed on before the journey to stop that from happening, so they exist to head off damage rather than to look well. That is what preventive means.

whyWrong.A: Temporary describes how long the plates last, not what they are for, and the contrast with ornamental calls for a purpose.
whyWrong.B: Traditional is about custom, and the passage explains the plates by the economics of a lame animal.
whyWrong.C: Expense is never mentioned; the only cost described is the awkwardness of shoeing a roped ox.

tips: When the blank is contrasted with ornamental, the word you want names a practical purpose.

whyCorrect: The underlined sentence states the naming rule: toward London is up and away from London is down, regardless of compass direction. The sentence after it works out what that meant in practice, one Exeter coach running up in the morning and down at night, and a clerk knowing which list to consult without learning anything about north or south. So the underlined sentence supplies the convention that the rest of the text then explains the effect of.

whyWrong.A: The text presents the system as useful to a booking clerk rather than as misleading, and it passes no criticism.
whyWrong.B: The Exeter coach is the example, and it appears in the sentence after the underlined one.
whyWrong.C: No office is identified anywhere; the text mentions only a booking clerk consulting lists.

tips: If the sentence names a rule and the next sentence shows the rule in use, the function is to state the rule.

whyCorrect: The text gives the guard's position and orders, alone at the back over the locked bags, armed, and instructed to stay with the mail rather than help the passengers. It then reports that the gun was fired perhaps a dozen times in the service's whole history and ends by saying its work was done while it stayed in its case. That last line makes the purpose plain: the arms and orders existed to discourage interference, not to be exercised.

whyWrong.B: The passage says the opposite, that the guard was not a passenger's servant and was to let them shift for themselves.
whyWrong.C: A dozen firings in the whole history of the service argues that robbery was rare, not common.
whyWrong.D: No changes over time are described; the equipment is presented as it stood.

commonMistakes: Treating the dozen firings as evidence that the gun was useless. The final sentence tells you deterrence counts as the gun working.

whyCorrect: The problem is that the worst weight loss came in the final week, when the roads were hard and the grazing near town poor. The dealers' answer was to buy short of the market and rent pasture for a month, so the beast arrived at the salesman rested and recovered. The last sentence states it directly: the animal was sold on the condition it had recovered, not the condition it had arrived in.

whyWrong.B: The cattle still covered the whole route; the text says the animal had made the whole journey, only not lately.
whyWrong.C: The entire practice depends on the weight being regained, so this contradicts the passage.
whyWrong.D: No price advantage is mentioned. The reason given is the condition of the animal at sale.

tips: Test a main-idea choice against the last sentence, which in this passage restates the thesis in different words.

whyCorrect: The text explains a practice and its payoff. The ironwork was varnished black and baked, producing a coat hard enough to resist a boot nail and unbroken enough to keep water off the metal, and the closing comparison gives the result: bright fittings looked well for a fortnight while baked ones survived a winter of salt and grit. The point is the protection the treatment gave.

whyWrong.A: Steps and handles are examples in a list that also includes stay bars and lamp brackets, and nothing says other parts needed no protection.
whyWrong.C: Being conspicuous is never mentioned; the reason given is durability against wear and water.
whyWrong.D: Baking is described as what makes the coat hard, not as a way of saving time.

commonMistakes: Choosing a plausible historical reason the text never gives. Stay inside the comparison the passage actually draws.

whyCorrect: The builder's claim is that the saving came from the body and not from what hung beneath it, so you need both columns. The body falls from 412 kg to 344 kg, a drop of 68 kg, while the springs and underframe stay between 265 and 268 kg, a spread of only 3 kg. One column changes sharply and the other hardly moves, which is exactly the separation the claim requires.

whyWrong.A: The two columns did not fall by similar proportions; if they had, the builder's claim would be refuted rather than supported.
whyWrong.B: The underframe figures do not fall steadily; they go 268, 266, 265, 267, which is drift rather than a trend.
whyWrong.C: The lightest body was built in 1838, when the underframe weighed 267 kg, not the heaviest figure in the column, and a coincidence of extremes would not show where the saving came from anyway.

tips: A claim of the form "the change came from A, not B" needs A moving and B holding still, so read both columns.

whyCorrect: Vargas's claim is that the drover's standing, not the cattle, was the real capital, because a written order is worthless unless both ends trust the man carrying it. A licensing system that admitted only settled householders over thirty and refused anyone with a proved debt is a mechanism for certifying exactly that standing, which shows the trade was organised around trustworthiness.

whyWrong.B: A rising head count measures the scale of the trade and says nothing about what made the paper payments work.
whyWrong.C: The width of drove roads is a physical detail with no bearing on credit or reputation.
whyWrong.D: Wool merchants using similar orders shows the instrument was common; it does not show that the drover's standing was what backed it.

tips: Support for a claim about reputation should be evidence that reputation was formally checked, enforced, or paid for.

whyCorrect: The researchers asked whether work at the walk changes the rate of hoof growth, so the relevant data are the two group means side by side. The exercised group grew 29 mm and the rested group 28 mm in twelve weeks, a difference of a single millimetre across four horses each, which is the comparison the question calls for.

whyWrong.A: The rested group grew 28 mm, so it is simply false that it grew no horn.
whyWrong.B: Neither figure exceeds 40 mm; both are under 30 mm.
whyWrong.D: Twenty-nine against twenty-eight is nearly identical, not double; that misreads the table.

commonMistakes: Expecting the data to show an effect. A near-identical pair of means is still the relevant comparison, and here it is the whole of the finding.

whyCorrect: The passage names one cause, a floor never dried out that holds wet bedding and dung against the sole, and one cure, a dry standing with the cleft opened and cleaned. If several horses in the same building show the condition at once, the thing they share is the building, not anything about themselves. So the groom should conclude the stable is at fault.

whyWrong.A: Nothing in the text describes transmission between animals; the cause given is a wet standing acting on each foot separately.
whyWrong.C: Shoeing is never mentioned, and the condition is explained entirely by the state of the floor.
whyWrong.D: The passage says the trouble clears when the horse is moved to a dry standing, so leaving the standing unchanged is not expected to help.

tips: When several cases appear together, look for the thing they all share; here it is the building named in the question itself.

whyCorrect: The text says the mile-stone clause was not a courtesy, then explains what it did: stones in place showed how many miles the trust was charging for, and a traveller counting stones since the last gate could see whether the toll matched the distance. That is a way for the public to verify what the trust claimed, which is what this choice states.

whyWrong.B: The number of gates is never limited by the clause; the passage discusses what the stones let a traveller check.
whyWrong.C: No resistance from travellers appears in the text, and the stones are presented as useful to them.
whyWrong.D: The stones are a public record in addition to whatever the trust kept, and nothing suggests other records became unnecessary.

commonMistakes: Reading the stones as merely helpful signposts when the passage explicitly rules out the courtesy interpretation.

whyCorrect: "The proprietors' winter bills lengthened the allowance between changes by a quarter of an hour and dropped one stage altogether on the highest ground" is a complete sentence, and "the amended bill was published in October" is another. Two independent clauses joined by "and" take a comma before the conjunction.

whyWrong.A: With no comma the two full clauses are run together, and the reader first takes "the amended bill" as a third object of the verbs.
whyWrong.B: A comma with no conjunction between independent clauses is a comma splice.
whyWrong.C: A colon introduces an explanation or list and is not used before a coordinating conjunction.

tips: Long compound verbs earlier in the sentence do not change the rule; test whether the words after the blank form a sentence of their own.

whyCorrect: "It was a right of way forty or fifty yards wide between banks, with grass over the whole of it" is a complete sentence, and "the width was the point, since two hundred beasts moving abreast at a walk fed as they went" is another. Joining two independent clauses with "and" requires a comma before it.

whyWrong.A: No punctuation before "and" leaves the two clauses run together.
whyWrong.B: A semicolon already joins independent clauses, so pairing it with "and" gives two connectors where one is needed.
whyWrong.C: A colon is not used before a coordinating conjunction, and the second clause develops rather than announces.

commonMistakes: Being distracted by the phrase "with grass over the whole of it"; the first clause is complete before it and stays complete with it.

whyCorrect: Both sides of the blank are independent clauses: "one movement did two things" and "it also meant that a worn lock left the step hanging." A semicolon is the mark that joins two independent clauses without a conjunction, and the adverb "unhappily" simply opens the second one.

whyWrong.B: A comma between two independent clauses with no conjunction is a comma splice.
whyWrong.C: With no punctuation the two clauses run together.
whyWrong.D: A colon followed by a coordinating conjunction is not a standard construction, and the second clause does not deliver what the first announced.

tips: An adverb such as unhappily, however, or therefore cannot join clauses; the punctuation before it still has to do the work.

whyCorrect: The subject of the sentence is "The colour that runs across a brightened face of quenched steel," and its verb is "tells." Nothing may separate a subject from its verb, so the blank takes no punctuation at all.

whyWrong.A: A colon would cut the sentence between subject and verb and leave "tells him its temperature" without a subject.
whyWrong.C: A single comma between a subject and its verb is not permitted, however long the subject is.
whyWrong.D: A semicolon needs an independent clause on each side, and the subject alone is not one.

commonMistakes: Inserting a comma because the subject is long. Length never licenses a break between subject and verb.

whyCorrect: The clause already has its subject and verb in "anything above the limit ... paid an extra toll." The blank begins a phrase describing how the toll was worked out, so it needs a past participle that modifies "toll": an extra toll reckoned by the hundredweight over it.

whyWrong.B: "Reckoning" is the active participle, which would say the toll did the reckoning rather than being reckoned.
whyWrong.C: "Reckons" is a finite verb, giving the clause a second main verb with no conjunction to join it.
whyWrong.D: "Was reckoned" also makes a second finite verb, producing a comma-free run-on with "paid."

tips: If the clause already has a main verb, the blank almost always needs a participle, not another finite verb.

whyCorrect: The subject is a three-part compound joined by "and": carts carrying manure, wagons going to and from a church, and horses drawing a hearse. A compound subject is plural, and the sentence is in the past, so the verb is were.

whyWrong.B: "Was" is singular and agrees only with the last item, not with the compound subject as a whole.
whyWrong.C: "Has been" is singular and present perfect, which clashes with both the number and the past-tense narrative.
whyWrong.D: "Is" is singular and present, wrong on both counts.

tips: When several noun phrases are joined by and before the verb, treat them as one plural subject.

whyCorrect: The subject of the final clause is "a shop," singular, with "that employed both" a relative clause describing it. The passage is written in the past tense, so the verb is was.

whyWrong.A: "Being" is a participle and leaves the clause with no finite verb.
whyWrong.B: "Are" is plural and present, agreeing with neither the singular subject nor the past-tense narration.
whyWrong.D: "Were" is plural, chosen by treating "both" or "two separate trades" as the subject rather than "a shop."

commonMistakes: Letting the word "both" pull the verb into the plural; it is the object of "employed," not the subject.

whyCorrect: The first sentence describes the famous long-distance coaches that made the newspapers. The second describes what most vehicles actually did, short local runs carrying clerks and market women who never appeared in any account. The second corrects the impression left by the first, so the transition has to be contrastive.

whyWrong.A: "Therefore" would make the local traffic a consequence of the trunk coaches, which it is not.
whyWrong.B: "Likewise" claims the two sentences describe similar things, but their whole point is the difference in scale and visibility.
whyWrong.C: "For instance" would make the local coaches an example of the trunk coaches, and they are the opposite case.

tips: When the second sentence begins with a word like "most" and describes the unglamorous majority, expect a contrast with the famous minority.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences give a problem and the trusts' answer: lanes let travellers dodge the gate, so trusts hung extra bars and chains across them. The third states the outcome, one gate on the map and often three on the ground, two of them catching only people trying to avoid payment. That is the result of the practice just described.

whyWrong.A: "For example" would introduce an instance of the previous sentence, but this sentence sums up what the practice produced.
whyWrong.C: "By contrast" needs an opposition, and the third sentence agrees with and follows from the second.
whyWrong.D: "Even so" signals a result that holds despite the previous sentence, whereas this one is caused by it.

tips: A sentence that counts up what the previous practice led to is a result, not an example.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences explain that no one proprietor could horse two hundred miles, so a line was divided among several, each taking a share of the miles and the receipts. The third draws the conclusion: such a coach was several businesses in succession, and a quarrel between any two stopped the service. The transition marks that conclusion.

whyWrong.B: "Nevertheless" would mean the conclusion holds in spite of the division, when it follows directly from it.
whyWrong.C: "In contrast" requires two things being set against each other, and this sentence describes the same arrangement from another angle.
whyWrong.D: "For instance" introduces a particular case, but no particular coach or line is named here.

tips: If the last sentence tells you what the arrangement amounted to, the transition is a conclusion word.

whyCorrect: The goal is how a common find becomes a dating tool, so the sentence has to show the two-step logic: a dated layer fixes a pattern to a period, and that pattern then dates other layers. Only this choice contains both steps and the features that carry the pattern, the nail holes and the edge finish.

whyWrong.A: That the details changed over time is a precondition for dating but does not show how the dating is done.
whyWrong.B: Survival in the ground explains why shoes are available to study, not how they date anything.
whyWrong.C: How common the finds are speaks to how often the method can be used, not to the method itself.

tips: A "how it works" goal needs the sequence of steps, so look for the choice with two linked clauses rather than a single fact.

whyCorrect: The goal names a problem in the older yards and a fix in the later ones, so both must appear. This choice gives the problem, a coach that could not be turned and had to be pushed out by hand, and the remedy, a second opening allowing it to drive straight through.

whyWrong.A: The narrow archway sets the scene but names neither the difficulty it caused nor the later solution.
whyWrong.B: That four men could push an empty body describes how the old workaround was managed, not how the problem was removed.
whyWrong.D: Taking off the horses and pushing the coach out is the old procedure with no mention of the later yards.

commonMistakes: Choosing a note that describes the old practice. The goal asks for the contrast between old and new, so the answer must reach the fix.

whyCorrect: The goal is why owners were told to leave the hood alone in the cold, so the sentence needs the physical cause and the cost of ignoring it. This choice supplies both: stiff leather cracks at the folds, and a cracked fold meant a whole new hood, which is why the warning existed.

whyWrong.A: How the hoops fold explains the mechanism of the hood and gives no reason to leave it down in frost.
whyWrong.C: Dressing the folds with tallow is a separate precaution and does not explain the warning.
whyWrong.D: Describing what the hood is made of provides background only.

tips: The strongest answer to a "why were they told to" goal usually names both the damage and its consequence.

whyCorrect: The middle sentence is explicit: nothing was added by the rubbing, a little was taken off each time, until the ground was perfectly level. The phrase "in the most literal sense" tells you to take the word at face value, so the blank has to name a process that works by removal. That is subtractive.

whyWrong.A: Provisional means temporary or standing in for something else, but each rubbed coat is a permanent part of the finish.
whyWrong.C: Decorative describes the aim of the varnish, and the sentence is about how the rubbing worked, not what it was for.
whyWrong.D: Hurried contradicts a dozen coats each rubbed back by hand.

tips: "In the most literal sense" is a signal that the missing word describes the physical mechanism, not a figurative quality.

whyCorrect: The passage defines the word as it uses it: a road was divided into lengths of eight to twelve miles, each ending at an inn with a fresh team, and a hill or an easy run made one length shorter or longer. A stage is therefore a stretch of the route between changes of horses.

whyWrong.A: A phase of development is the everyday figurative sense and does not fit a distance measured in miles between inns.
whyWrong.B: A stagecoach is a vehicle, but the sentence says the stage "was measured," which only a distance can be.
whyWrong.D: A raised platform is the theatrical meaning and has nothing to do with roads or teams.

commonMistakes: Reaching for the most familiar meaning of a word instead of the one the sentence can accommodate grammatically.

whyCorrect: The hot shoe scorches the horn wherever it stands proud, and the mark it leaves shows the smith exactly where more metal has to come off. That mark is information about the fit obtained by a physical test, so the blank names what the practice supplies: evidence.

whyWrong.B: A warning implies danger ahead, but the scorch mark reports a present state, where the shoe is touching.
whyWrong.C: Reassurance would mean confirming the fit is good, whereas the mark's value is in showing where the fit is bad.
whyWrong.D: Authority concerns the smith's standing rather than anything he learns about this particular foot.

tips: Ask what the practice gives the smith that cold fitting does not; here it is a readable record of contact.

whyCorrect: The leather brace gives a soft ride but stretches with use and has to be taken up again and again. Steel returns to its shape and does not lengthen over a season. The final sentence trades the soft motion for its opposite property, so the blank names what steel keeps and leather does not: a motion that stays the same over time.

whyWrong.A: Noise is never mentioned in the comparison.
whyWrong.B: Cost is not discussed, and in any case the blank describes the motion, not the price.
whyWrong.D: Gentle is the quality of the leather that the builders gave up, so it cannot also be what they gained.

commonMistakes: Picking a word that repeats what was given up. "In return for" requires the blank to name the other side of the trade.

whyCorrect: The dogs travelled unaccompanied and stopped at the same inns the droves had used, where a meal was already expected and charged to the master. That only works if the same route had been walked so often that both the dogs and the innkeepers knew it, which is what habitual means.

whyWrong.A: Length is not the issue; the journey is three hundred miles either way, and shortness would not tell a dog where to eat.
whyWrong.B: Nothing suggests the road was patrolled, and protection would not explain the meals at the inns.
whyWrong.C: Gradient plays no part in the account; the dogs needed familiarity, not easy going.

tips: When an arrangement depends on both parties knowing what to expect, the blank usually names repetition or custom.

whyCorrect: The first sentence says the body was drawn full size in chalk on the shop floor. The underlined sentence explains why that was worth doing: a curve that looks well at an inch to the foot can look heavy at full size, and the only way to judge it is to stand back from the full-size drawing. It supplies the justification for the practice just described.

whyWrong.A: It says the small drawing can mislead, which is the opposite of conceding that it was more accurate.
whyWrong.B: The patterns and the thin board appear in the next sentence, not the underlined one.
whyWrong.C: Only one shop and one method are described anywhere in the text.

tips: A sentence beginning with a problem that the previous practice avoids is almost always giving the reason for that practice.

whyCorrect: The text sets out two answers to one question. The first engineer treats the road as a structure carrying the load in its stone. The underlined sentence gives the rival principle, that dry subsoil carries the load and the surface only sheds water. The closing sentence then lists what follows from it: less stone, lower cost, and complete dependence on open ditches.

whyWrong.A: No claim is made that hand-set stone disappeared; the text presents two contemporary approaches.
whyWrong.C: It states a different principle rather than admitting a fault in the first one.
whyWrong.D: It contradicts the first method rather than restating it, since it denies that the pavement carries the load.

tips: When a text says two answers were given, expect one sentence for each principle and the rest for consequences.

whyCorrect: The passage explains that horn keeps growing at about a centimetre a month whether or not a shoe is on, so after five or six weeks the foot has grown past the iron. The shoe is then taken off long before it is worn out, and the closing sentence states the conclusion, that the smith's round is set by horn growth rather than iron wear.

whyWrong.A: Workload is never linked to growth rate; the figure given is a steady centimetre a month.
whyWrong.B: The text says the shoe stops the wall wearing but does nothing to stop it growing.
whyWrong.D: The passage says the opposite, that shoes come off long before they are worn out.

tips: When the last sentence contains a "rather than," it is usually stating the main idea as a contrast.

whyCorrect: The passage says the extra fare bought less than it appears, then makes the case: four inside sat knee to knee with the windows shut, while eleven outside had air and a view. The reason inside places still sold first is given in the last clause, that people who could pay more would not be seen on the roof. So the fare bought questionable comfort and sold mainly on what it signified.

whyWrong.A: The text argues that the comfort was doubtful, describing a cramped box with closed windows.
whyWrong.B: No claim is made about demand for outside places; eleven of them were carried and the passage never says they went unsold.
whyWrong.C: Proprietors filled the inside first, so they plainly wanted to sell those places.

commonMistakes: Assuming the more expensive option must be the better one; this passage exists to deny that.

whyCorrect: Two explanations are in play, road concussion and heavy feeding, so a test of the concussion account has to change the road surface while holding feed constant. Choice C does exactly that: the same horses on the same feed develop the condition far less often once they leave stone roads for soft ground, which isolates concussion as the operating cause.

whyWrong.A: Horses at grass differ from coach horses in work as well as surface, so this removes the concussion but does not test it cleanly; at best it weakens the feeding account.
whyWrong.B: A shoe that relieves the condition speaks to treatment, not to what caused it in the first place.
whyWrong.D: A seasonal pattern appearing on every kind of road points away from road surface, since surface is the one thing not varying with it.

tips: To support one of two rival causes, look for the finding that varies that cause alone and holds the other fixed.

whyCorrect: Nwosu says the chapter restrains the tool and assumes the beginner will do too much. The quotation in choice A does both: it warns that horn taken off does not grow back and that a hand busy above the clenches has already gone too far. That is a caution against excess, not an instruction in technique.

whyWrong.B: Holding the rasp level with a low elbow is exactly the teaching of use that Nwosu says the chapter is not chiefly doing.
whyWrong.C: A recommended tool length is a practical specification with no warning in it.
whyWrong.D: The tool's history says nothing about how much a beginner should use it.

tips: Match the quotation to the claim's specific shape; here the claim is about restraint, so look for a warning rather than a method.

whyCorrect: The committee claims traffic was growing while receipts fell for a reason other than lost trade. The table shows exactly that divergence: vehicles counted rise 18,400, 19,100, 20,300, 21,600 while money taken falls 742, 705, 661, 618. Traffic up in every year with takings down in every year is the pattern the claim needs.

whyWrong.A: The highest count, in 1843, goes with the lowest sum, 618 pounds, so this misreads the table.
whyWrong.C: The vehicle count did not fall after 1840; it rose every year.
whyWrong.D: The money taken did not rise at all, so describing it as rising more slowly misstates the data.

commonMistakes: Reading only one column. The claim is about two measures moving in opposite directions, so both have to be checked.

whyCorrect: The passage says a smith can move the point of contact by resetting the shoe, but that a horse working at speed will cut itself again before the alteration takes effect. The boot is strapped over the spot, so it exists to cover the gap in time between making the change and the change working.

whyWrong.A: The boot does not correct the swing at all; the passage credits the reshoeing with changing where the foot lands.
whyWrong.B: The text says a smith can alter the setting, so this contradicts it.
whyWrong.C: Nothing links the injury to unshod horses; the horses discussed are being reshod.

tips: When a passage says a remedy is slow to act, a second measure is usually there to cover the interval.

whyCorrect: The posting house supplied horses and a postboy by the mile to someone travelling in his own carriage, and the boy rode one of the pair so the traveller's own servant kept his seat. Horses were hired only as far as the next house and paid for only for the outward miles. That fits a traveller who wanted to keep his carriage and his servants but not to maintain horses along the whole road.

whyWrong.B: The postboys came with the horses and were not engaged by the traveller, so the arrangement works against this preference.
whyWrong.C: The system required stopping at every posting house to change horses.
whyWrong.D: The service assumes the traveller has his own carriage; only horses and a boy were supplied.

commonMistakes: Overlooking the detail that the carriage belongs to the traveller, which rules out the choice about hiring one.

whyCorrect: "He learned to make a shoe in the first two years" and "the remaining five went on the foot itself" are both complete sentences, and no coordinating conjunction is offered to join them. A semicolon is the mark that joins two independent clauses on its own.

whyWrong.A: A colon is not used before a coordinating conjunction, and the second clause continues the account rather than explaining the first.
whyWrong.C: A comma alone between independent clauses is a comma splice.
whyWrong.D: With no punctuation the clauses run together and "two years the remaining five" reads as a single confused phrase.

tips: If none of the choices offers a conjunction you could use with a comma, the answer is usually the semicolon.

whyCorrect: Both sides of the blank are complete sentences, and "yet" is a coordinating conjunction, so a comma before it is the correct join. It also gives the right sense, since a custom worth more than the wage was nonetheless never written down.

whyWrong.B: Without the comma, two independent clauses are joined by a bare conjunction; a comma is required before a coordinating conjunction linking full clauses.
whyWrong.C: "However" is a conjunctive adverb, not a conjunction, so a comma on each side of it leaves the clauses spliced.
whyWrong.D: A colon introduces an explanation or a list and is not used before a coordinating conjunction.

commonMistakes: Treating however and yet as interchangeable. They mean nearly the same thing but are punctuated differently.

whyCorrect: "Because the stuffing settled unevenly in the first month, a trimmer expected the work to come back to him" is a complete sentence, and "he charged for the second visit in his original estimate" is another. A semicolon joins them, and "accordingly" then opens the second clause as an adverb.

whyWrong.A: With no punctuation the two clauses run together, and "to him accordingly he charged" gives the reader no boundary.
whyWrong.B: A colon followed by "and" is not a standard construction, and the colon would be doing the same work as the conjunction.
whyWrong.D: A comma between two independent clauses is a splice; "accordingly" is an adverb and cannot join them.

tips: Words like accordingly, therefore, and however need a semicolon or a full stop before them when they open a new clause.

whyCorrect: "In the narrow stalls a horse stood tied and faced the wall" is a complete sentence and "in the loose boxes at the far end it could turn and lie down" is another, each opening with its own place phrase. With no conjunction available, the semicolon is the mark that joins them.

whyWrong.B: A comma between two independent clauses with no conjunction is a comma splice.
whyWrong.C: Without punctuation the clauses run together and "faced the wall in the loose boxes" briefly reads as one place.
whyWrong.D: A colon before a coordinating conjunction is not standard, and the second clause contrasts with the first rather than explaining it.

tips: Two clauses that each begin with a prepositional phrase of place still need a full stop or semicolon between them.

whyCorrect: The blank is the verb of the second half of a compound clause: a boat took a rope and the rest of the herd followed behind it. The passage is narrated in the past, as "took" and "were walked" show, so the verb must be the simple past.

whyWrong.A: "Follows" shifts to the present and breaks the tense established by "took."
whyWrong.C: "Following" is a participle, leaving the clause with no finite verb.
whyWrong.D: "To follow" is an infinitive and likewise cannot be the clause's main verb.

tips: Match the tense to the nearest finite verb in the same sentence, here "took."

whyCorrect: With a neither/nor subject the verb agrees with the part nearer to it, and the nearer part here is "the brass channels," which is plural. The passage is also in the past tense, so the verb is were.

whyWrong.A: "Has been" is singular and present perfect, wrong in both number and tense.
whyWrong.B: "Is" is singular and present.
whyWrong.D: "Was" is singular; it would agree with "the glass," but that is the farther of the two elements, not the nearer.

tips: For neither ... nor and either ... or, look at the element immediately before the verb to decide number.

whyCorrect: The clause already has its subject and verb in "he lever the iron away," and what follows the comma describes how that is done. It also has to be parallel with "dragging them through it" later in the same phrase, so the blank takes the -ing participle: drawing.

whyWrong.A: "Drew" is a finite past verb, which both breaks the parallel with "dragging" and adds a second main verb.
whyWrong.B: "Draws" is likewise finite and leaves the sentence with two main verbs and no conjunction.
whyWrong.C: "To draw" is not parallel with "dragging" and turns the phrase into a statement of purpose rather than of manner.

tips: When a "rather than" pairs two forms, both sides must match; here "dragging" fixes the form the blank has to take.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences describe the operation step by step: the nail comes out above the ground, the point is cut off, and the stub is turned down and hammered into a bed. The third sentence states what that procedure achieves, a grip between head and turned end with nothing entering the sensitive foot. The transition has to say that the result follows from the method just described.

whyWrong.A: "Meanwhile" marks two things happening at once, but this is the outcome of the steps, not a parallel event.
whyWrong.C: "By contrast" needs an opposing case, and no alternative method is mentioned.
whyWrong.D: "Admittedly" concedes a point against the argument, whereas this sentence states its success.

tips: When the last sentence describes the result of a described procedure, look for a transition meaning by that method.

whyCorrect: The opening sentence promises a difference that mattered. The second describes the hind boot, low down and out of the wind; the third describes the imperial on the roof, where weight raises the centre of gravity of a tall narrow vehicle. The two are opposed in position and in effect, so the transition marks contrast.

whyWrong.A: "Consequently" would make the roof case follow from the hind boot, but they are alternatives.
whyWrong.B: "Likewise" claims similarity, and the first sentence has already announced a difference.
whyWrong.C: "In short" introduces a summary, and the third sentence gives new information about a second location.

tips: An opening sentence promising that a difference mattered tells you the transition later on will be contrastive.

whyCorrect: The second sentence says Parliament let the acts lapse one at a time instead of repealing them together. The third says the change had no single date and that people argued afterwards about when the system ended. A gradual, piecemeal ending is exactly what produces an uncertain date, so the third sentence is a consequence of the second.

whyWrong.A: "Similarly" needs two comparable cases, and this sentence draws out an implication instead.
whyWrong.B: "For example" would introduce an instance, but the absence of a single date is a general consequence, not a case.
whyWrong.D: "Nonetheless" signals a result that defies what came before, when this one follows straight from it.

commonMistakes: Reading the disagreement among contemporaries as surprising; it is precisely what a piecemeal expiry would cause.

whyCorrect: The goal is how the rules made it safe to hand a stranger a herd, so the answer must connect the licence conditions to the owner's confidence. This choice does: it names the screening, a settled householder over thirty with no proved debt, and the penalty that backed it, an unlicensed driver being liable to be treated as a thief, and states the effect on the owner.

whyWrong.B: What a licensed drover was allowed to do describes the trade rather than what made it safe.
whyWrong.C: That a licence was needed leaves out both the conditions attached to it and the sanction behind it.
whyWrong.D: The age and householder requirement is one condition among several and stops short of the owner's position.

tips: When the goal names a result, check the choice actually states that result rather than leaving it to be inferred.

whyCorrect: To emphasise the size of the improvement you need the two times set against each other. Sixteen hours against thirty-eight on the same road is a direct comparison, and it is the only choice that gives both figures.

whyWrong.B: The spread of the service shows it was judged a success but puts no number on the gain.
whyWrong.C: The five miles an hour of the old post gives the starting point with nothing to compare it against.
whyWrong.D: Who proposed the scheme is background and says nothing about how much faster it was.

commonMistakes: Choosing the note with the most striking single number. An improvement needs a before and an after.

whyCorrect: The goal is that the patterns differ because the work differs, so each shoe has to be paired with the job it does. This choice does that twice over: the wide flat shoe with the horse pushing into the collar, and the narrower bevelled shoe with the animal breaking over the toe at speed.

whyWrong.A: The draught shoe alone gives a shape with no work attached and no comparison.
whyWrong.C: The saddle shoe alone has the same fault from the other side.
whyWrong.D: That both are made from one bar by the same operations stresses what the two patterns share, which is the opposite of the goal.

tips: A "differ because" goal needs both halves of each pair, shape and reason, for both items.

whyCorrect: The passage says a drover planned the day's march around where the paid enclosures lay rather than around a distance he would have chosen. The blank completes "the distance he would have liked to," and the thing you do with a day's distance is travel it, so the word is cover.

whyWrong.A: Avoiding a distance makes no sense as an aim, since he needs to travel toward market.
whyWrong.B: Measuring a distance is not what the sentence contrasts with stopping at enclosures.
whyWrong.C: Shortening reverses the sense; the constraint is where he must stop, not a wish to travel less.

tips: Read the blank as part of the whole phrase; "the distance he would have liked to ___" only takes a verb of travelling.

whyCorrect: The passage says ash worked green opens at every joint, so builders stacked the timber and left it a year for every inch of thickness. That waiting time cannot be compressed without bringing back the fault, and the sentence calls it the one part of the process that resisted something. What it resists is being speeded up, that is, hastened.

whyWrong.A: Delegating means handing the work to someone else, but seasoning is not work anyone performs.
whyWrong.C: Recording the delay would be easy and is never presented as a difficulty.
whyWrong.D: Pricing is not at issue; the passage discusses time, not cost.

commonMistakes: Choosing a word about the workshop's organisation when the sentence is about the one thing time alone controls.

whyCorrect: The contrast in the sentence is between two rates. The higher rate includes the office making good a loss, while the ordinary rate covers the underlined word only, with the sender bearing the risk. What remains once insurance is stripped away is the act of carrying the parcel, so the word means transport.

whyWrong.B: The vehicle sense would say the rate covered a coach, which nobody bought by the parcel.
whyWrong.C: Posture is the bodily sense of the word and has no place in a discussion of rates.
whyWrong.D: Expense would make the sentence say the rate covered the cost, which is circular; the rate is the cost.

tips: For a word-in-context question, work out what the sentence needs the word to contrast with, here the insurance the higher rate provided.

whyCorrect: The middle sentence describes a mechanism: the weight of the horse presses the wedge flat, the foot spreads, and blood is squeezed out of the veins and up the leg. That is a device moving fluid, which is a pump, and the closing phrase about the heart not replacing it confirms the sense, since the heart is the body's other pump.

whyWrong.A: A measure would record something rather than move blood, and nothing here is being measured.
whyWrong.B: A signal would carry information, but the wedge does mechanical work on the blood itself.
whyWrong.D: A guard fits the cushion idea the first sentence explicitly sets aside as insufficient.

tips: The mention of the heart at the end is the clue; the blank has to name something the heart also is.

whyCorrect: The passage describes a carrier settling with the lessee for a lump sum covering a quarter or a year and then passing as often as he likes, with gains named on both sides. The word therefore refers to that arrangement between the two parties, an agreement, and the final sentence extends the same arrangement across several gates.

whyWrong.A: There is no quarrel in the passage; the parties are described as both gaining.
whyWrong.C: A mixture is the chemical sense of the word and has nothing to do with tolls.
whyWrong.D: An essay is the schoolroom sense and cannot be made between a carrier and a lessee.

commonMistakes: Picking the most familiar meaning of a technical term instead of the one the surrounding sentences define.

whyCorrect: The text describes two openings in the anvil's heel, one holding a cutting tool upright and one giving a punch somewhere to go. It then says neither does any work itself and that both exist so the smith's two hands, one holding and one striking, are enough. The purpose is to show how those features let a single worker manage the job.

whyWrong.B: The opening remark about the face is a way into the description, not a claim about what smiths believe.
whyWrong.C: Punching and cutting are mentioned as the jobs the holes serve, but no sequence of making a shoe is set out.
whyWrong.D: No other trade's anvil appears in the text.

tips: The final sentence of a short text often states its purpose outright; check your answer against it before committing.

whyCorrect: The first sentence sets up the problem, that tolls at every gate would swallow the value of the drove. The rest explains the answer: routes that cross turnpikes at right angles and otherwise run on ridgeways and commons outside any trust's authority. The closing line lists what those routes gave, extra miles but softer going for beasts that had to arrive fit to sell, and no charge, so the trade-off is the point.

whyWrong.A: The passage says the drove routes were the longer ones, so length is a cost of the choice rather than a reason for it.
whyWrong.B: The routes were worked out by drovers to escape the trusts, not laid out by the trusts.
whyWrong.D: Trusts plainly could charge for cattle; that is the whole reason the drovers avoided their gates.

tips: When a passage lists what a choice cost and what it saved, the main idea is usually that the saving outweighed the cost.

whyCorrect: The complaint about the old duty is not that the labour was insufficient but that it came in the weeks the fields could spare men, which were not the weeks the roads needed work. Commuting the duty to money let the trust hire labour whenever mending was worth doing, so the passage ends with the road mended in the right season. The gain is freedom from the farming calendar.

whyWrong.A: No shortage of men is described, and the duty is commuted rather than abolished.
whyWrong.B: The passage says the paying parish found its road mended, not neglected.
whyWrong.D: No resistance is mentioned, and the parish is described as discharging its obligation in an hour.

commonMistakes: Assuming the reform was about money. The text's complaint and its remedy are both about timing.

whyCorrect: Each element of the description points the same way: a private act naming one stretch and one local body, borrowing secured on that road's gates and spendable on that stretch and no other, expiry after twenty-one years without a fresh act, and hundreds of such bodies answerable to no one else. That is a separate, temporary body confined to its own piece of road.

whyWrong.A: The text says a trust expired unless a fresh act renewed it, and says nothing about renewal being automatic.
whyWrong.C: It states the opposite: hundreds existed at once and none was answerable to any other.
whyWrong.D: Trusts could borrow on the security of what the gates took; that power is granted, not denied.

tips: When every detail in a passage restricts the same thing, the main idea is the restriction they add up to.

whyCorrect: Alleyne's claim has two halves: the reputation rested on the ostlers' drill, and not on the horses. The quotation in D supplies both, four men in position before the horn is heard, each to his own buckle and side, a coach away in ninety seconds, and horses no better than a farmer's. It is the only one that credits the drill while explicitly discounting the stock.

whyWrong.A: The number of pairs kept describes the scale of the yard, not what made it work.
whyWrong.B: Paving costs concern the premises and say nothing about either drill or horses.
whyWrong.C: Travellers speaking well of the house records the reputation without explaining what produced it.

tips: When a claim says "X rather than Y," the best quotation usually mentions both X and Y.

whyCorrect: The dispute is whether the reflector helps the driver see the verge or helps others see the coach. A finding that the plate sends almost all the light forward along the road while leaving the verge beside the wheels dark rules out the first purpose and fits the second, since light thrown ahead is light aimed at whoever is approaching.

whyWrong.A: Larger candles make the lamp brighter without saying anything about where the light is directed or why.
whyWrong.B: Mounting height might affect both purposes and does not separate them.
whyWrong.C: The material of the plate concerns how well it reflects, not which of the two jobs it was doing.

commonMistakes: Treating any detail about the lamp as evidence. The question is about direction of light, so only a finding about direction can settle it.

whyCorrect: Achebe says the surveyor blamed water rather than material. The quotation in B makes exactly that separation: where the ditch is choked the metal has broken up, and where the ditch runs, metal from the same quarry and the same year stands firm. Holding the stone constant and varying the drainage is the argument Achebe attributes to him.

whyWrong.A: A late payment from the parish is administrative and bears on neither drainage nor stone.
whyWrong.C: Harder stone than in 1836 is a remark about material, which is what Achebe says the report is not blaming.
whyWrong.D: A tonnage laid between two milestones is the kind of line that made the report look like a request for more stone.

tips: A quotation supports a causal claim best when it holds the rival cause constant, as this one does with quarry and year.

whyCorrect: The passage lists the non-visual cues a coachman used, the sound of the wheels as the metal changed, the horses slackening at an unseen rise, the smell of a wood at a turn. It then reports that a man on an unfamiliar road at night went slower than on his own road in fog, so the difference was knowledge of that road rather than how much he could see. The blank has to name that learned familiarity.

whyWrong.A: Passenger numbers are never mentioned and would apply equally on a familiar road.
whyWrong.B: Resurfacing would change the sound of the wheels but does not explain why a known road in fog was driven faster than an unknown one.
whyWrong.D: Lamps are a matter of visibility, which is exactly what the sentence says the speed did not depend on.

tips: The comparison in the last sentence tells you what to hold constant; fog removes sight but leaves familiarity intact.

whyCorrect: Sheep make eight or nine miles a day where bullocks make fifteen, so the same distance takes a sheep drove roughly twice as many days. Every extra day on the road is another night that has to be provided for, which is why the sheep drover reckoned in weeks. So the drove needed far more overnight stops for the same journey.

whyWrong.A: The passage says a flock spreads across the verge to graze as it goes, so it fed on the move rather than only at halts.
whyWrong.C: Condition is claimed only for the bullock, which is said to make fifteen miles without losing it; nothing is said about sheep arriving better.
whyWrong.D: Route availability by season is never discussed.

commonMistakes: Stopping at the slower pace. The question asks what the difference meant in practice, and the practical unit is the day's march.

whyCorrect: "A traveller arriving after that pulled a wire beside the door, which rang a bell over the bed itself" is a complete sentence, and "the keeper came down in whatever he had on, took the money by lamplight, and lifted the bar" is another. Two independent clauses joined by "and" take a comma before the conjunction.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon joins independent clauses by itself, so using it with "and" doubles the connector.
whyWrong.B: A colon is not used before a coordinating conjunction, and the second clause continues the sequence rather than explaining the first.
whyWrong.D: With no comma the two full clauses run together.

tips: The commas inside the final list do not change the rule; the join between the two clauses still needs its own comma.

whyCorrect: "Lenders advanced money on the security of what the gates would take" and "the interest on it was a first charge on those receipts" are both complete sentences. Joining them with "and" requires a comma before the conjunction.

whyWrong.A: A colon introduces an explanation or list and does not precede a coordinating conjunction.
whyWrong.C: Without the comma the two independent clauses run together.
whyWrong.D: A semicolon and "and" both perform the join, so together they are redundant.

commonMistakes: Thinking the length of the second clause calls for a stronger mark; a comma with the conjunction is the standard join however long the clause.

whyCorrect: Both sides of the blank are independent clauses: "A builder who shortened it gained a vehicle that turned in a narrower space" and "he also gained one that flexed under a heavy load." With no coordinating conjunction offered, the semicolon is the mark that joins them, and "unfortunately" simply opens the second clause.

whyWrong.A: With no punctuation, "a narrower space unfortunately he also gained" runs together and leaves the adverb attached to the wrong clause.
whyWrong.B: A colon followed by "and" is not standard, and the second clause opposes rather than explains the first.
whyWrong.D: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice; the adverb cannot join them.

tips: Adverbs like unfortunately, however, and moreover never join clauses, no matter how connective they feel.

whyCorrect: "The birds were driven first through soft tar and then through sand or grit, which set into a crust beneath each foot" is a complete sentence, and "The crust wore through in about a hundred miles and had to be renewed" is another. Separating them with a full stop is the only choice that joins two independent clauses correctly here.

whyWrong.A: A comma between two independent clauses with no conjunction is a comma splice.
whyWrong.B: Without punctuation the sentence runs on, and "each foot the crust" briefly reads as one phrase.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon already joins the clauses, so adding "and" gives two connectors at once.

tips: When the choices offer a comma, a bare join, a semicolon plus a conjunction, and a full stop, the full stop is usually the only clean option.

whyCorrect: The sentence already has its subject and verb in "The proprietors met and agreed." What follows the comma is a phrase describing the state they were in, built on the participle "having discovered," and such a phrase takes a bare subject with no finite verb: each having discovered that competition cost more than it gained.

whyWrong.A: "And" signals another clause, but "each of them having discovered" has no finite verb, so the sentence would join a clause to a fragment.
whyWrong.B: "Which" opens a relative clause that then never receives a finite verb, leaving the construction unfinished.
whyWrong.D: "Each of them were" supplies a finite verb, producing a second main clause spliced on with only a comma, and it also disagrees in number with the singular "each."

tips: A phrase built on "having done" is not a clause; it attaches to the main sentence without a conjunction and without its own tensed verb.

whyCorrect: The opening participial phrase "Planted beside a stance" has to attach to the subject of the main clause, and the thing planted is the three or four Scots pines. The clause needs a plural subject pronoun for the verb "told," which is they.

whyWrong.A: "Which" would make the whole thing a relative clause with no main clause left in the sentence.
whyWrong.C: "It" is singular and cannot refer back to three or four pines.
whyWrong.D: "These being" produces a participial phrase rather than a subject and verb, leaving the sentence with no main clause.

commonMistakes: Choosing a relative pronoun after an introductory phrase; the sentence still needs a subject for its main verb.

whyCorrect: Strip the modifier and the subject is "a shoe," singular, with "made with a bar across the heels" describing it. The passage speaks in the present about what such a shoe does, so the verb is throws.

whyWrong.A: "Throw" is the plural form; nothing plural is the subject.
whyWrong.B: "Throwing" is a participle and would leave the sentence with no main verb.
whyWrong.C: "Have thrown" is plural and puts the action in the perfect, which does not match the general present-tense statement.

tips: Cross out any participial phrase after the subject before checking agreement; "heels" is inside such a phrase and cannot govern the verb.

whyCorrect: The second sentence establishes that the heat is concentrated in a fist-sized spot directly over the single air nozzle. The third gives the smith's practice, banking the fuel around that spot and putting nothing in the fire he does not mean to heat. The practice follows from the physical fact, so the transition marks consequence.

whyWrong.B: "Nevertheless" would mean the practice holds despite the concentrated heat, but it is a response to it.
whyWrong.C: "In contrast" needs an opposing case, and no other kind of fire is being described at this point.
whyWrong.D: "Similarly" claims a parallel, whereas the third sentence draws a conclusion from the second.

tips: If the sentence after the blank describes what someone does about the fact just stated, the transition is causal.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences say the beasts were worth moving only after the summer grazing had fattened them, so September was the moment and June was too early. The third states what that produced on the ground, empty roads for most of the year and the whole season's traffic in about six weeks. That concentration is the consequence of the narrow window.

whyWrong.A: "Even so" would signal a result running against the previous sentences, but this one follows from them.
whyWrong.B: "By contrast" needs two things opposed, and this sentence extends the same point to the roads.
whyWrong.C: "In particular" narrows to a specific case, whereas this sentence generalises about the whole season.

tips: A narrow window for an activity almost always produces a concentrated result, which is a consequence, not a contrast.

whyCorrect: The second sentence gives the gathering great commercial weight: dealers from several counties, and a price that settled what beasts fetched hundreds of miles away. The third says it had almost no buildings, just a weighing shed and a clerk's booth. Small physical presence sits against large importance, so the transition is concessive.

whyWrong.A: "Likewise" claims the two sentences say similar things, but they pull in opposite directions.
whyWrong.B: "In other words" introduces a restatement, and the absence of buildings is new and different information.
whyWrong.D: "Accordingly" would make the lack of buildings follow from the gathering's importance, which is backwards.

commonMistakes: Missing that importance and permanence are being contrasted; the surprise is that so much trade needed so little building.

whyCorrect: The goal is why the report mattered to lenders, so the answer must connect what the report contained to a lender's interest. This choice does: repairs and their cost set against measurements at the same fixed points a year before, letting a lender see whether the road that secured his money was being maintained.

whyWrong.A: The surveyor's annual ride describes the procedure with no bearing on lenders.
whyWrong.B: Measuring at fixed points is one method within the report and stops short of what it showed anyone.
whyWrong.D: That the report was read before the accounts were passed concerns the trustees' meeting, not the lenders' interest.

tips: When the goal names an audience, the correct choice usually names that audience or its stake explicitly.

whyCorrect: The goal is how the waybill located missing money, so the sentence needs the record, the comparison, and the result. This choice has all three: every passenger and the stage at which each joined, the comparison with the money handed in, and a discrepancy pinned to one stage of one journey.

whyWrong.B: The contents of the sheet alone do not show how a shortfall was found.
whyWrong.C: The physical description of the sheet is background with no method in it.
whyWrong.D: The blank line for passengers picked up on the road is one detail of the record and does not describe the checking process.

tips: A "how it worked" goal needs the comparison step, not just the document being compared.

whyCorrect: The goal asks what the name identified for someone booking, so the answer must say what the name attached to. This choice states it directly: the name belonged to a service on a road rather than to a vehicle or an owner, so booking on a name was booking that service.

whyWrong.A: What happened when a proprietor sold out shows the name did not follow the owner, but it stops short of saying what a traveller was buying.
whyWrong.B: Names painted on door panels is a fact about decoration.
whyWrong.C: A list of famous names supplies examples without explaining what a name meant.

commonMistakes: Choosing the vivid list of names. Examples do not answer a question about what something identified.

whyCorrect: The passage describes cutting: squaring one face with a chisel, squaring the next to it, then cutting the mouldings against a zinc template. The underlined word covers all of that shaping done in a set order, so it means worked.

whyWrong.A: Arranged would refer to placing blocks in position, which happens later when the block is set in the wall.
whyWrong.B: Bandaged is the medical sense and has no application to stone.
whyWrong.C: Clothed is the everyday sense of the word and does not fit an object being cut to shape.

tips: A technical trade sense of a common word is usually recoverable from the actions the passage has just described.

whyCorrect: The clay going in is described as a mixture of stiff lumps, soft lumps, grit and air pockets. What comes out is the same clay throughout, with nothing left that would tear a moulded shape. The final sentence rules out softening as the aim, so the blank must name the consistency the mill produces: uniform.

whyWrong.A: Colour is never mentioned, and knives in a barrel do nothing to it.
whyWrong.C: Abundance concerns quantity, but the mill changes the condition of the clay rather than how much there is.
whyWrong.D: Watertightness would matter to the finished brick, not to clay being prepared for moulding.

tips: When a sentence says "not to X but to," the blank has to name a different result, and the passage has usually already described it.

whyCorrect: The sentence contrasts two things the bloom might show, the end of drying or the beginning of decay. That makes the word a matter of what the bloom tells you, not what it does to the wall, so it means indicates. The rest of the sentence agrees, since the crust is brushed off once and does not return.

whyWrong.A: Scores means cuts lines into a surface, and the salt sits on the face rather than cutting it.
whyWrong.B: Celebrates is the ceremonial sense of marking an occasion and is far too strong for a description of salt crystals.
whyWrong.C: Stains is tempting because the bloom is visible, but the sentence is weighing two interpretations of what the bloom signifies, and a stain is not a signal.

commonMistakes: Choosing the physical sense of a word when the sentence is asking what the thing shows rather than what it does.

whyCorrect: The passage says nothing holds the tile but a small projection hooked over a batten and the tile's own weight, which is why a roof can be stripped by hand and a single tile swapped out.
