That describes a covering that rests in place rather than being attached, so the word opposed to "fixed" here is hung, the very verb the first sentence uses.

whyWrong.B: Sealed would mean the joints are closed against water, and a tile roof works by overlap, not by seals.
whyWrong.C: Welded is a permanent metal join and contradicts lifting a tile out by hand.
whyWrong.D: Buried makes no sense of tiles that lie exposed on the outside of a roof.

tips: The blank is contrasted with "fixed," so look for a word meaning held without fastening; the passage's own verbs often supply it.

whyCorrect: The text concedes that a man's weight is a poor engine, then shows what the great wheel gave in return: a fivefold multiplication from the wheel and drum, and a steady pull without the jerks of a hauling team. The last clause names the job, lowering a stone over a finished vault, which needs control rather than brute force. So the text explains why a modest machine suited its work.

whyWrong.A: No geographical spread is described; the wheels are located in English churches and nowhere else is mentioned.
whyWrong.B: The text does not claim better power was unavailable; it argues this power was the right kind.
whyWrong.C: The churches are mentioned only as where the wheels survive, with no description of them.

tips: Note where a passage says "not X so much as Y"; that clause usually contains the purpose.

whyCorrect: The first sentence describes the old kiln, in which the flame naturally rises and overheats the top of the setting. The underlined sentence states the general principle that a gas follows the draught, up or down. The sentence after it describes the down-draught kiln, which relies on exactly that principle, sending flame up the walls and pulling it down through the setting to floor flues. So the underlined sentence supplies the principle the new arrangement depends on.

whyWrong.B: It admits no weakness; it states the fact that makes the new kiln workable.
whyWrong.C: No technical term from the previous sentence is defined; the term down-draught appears afterwards.
whyWrong.D: It does not question the older kiln's behaviour, which it leaves standing.

tips: A general statement wedged between a problem and a solution is usually the principle that licenses the solution.

whyCorrect: Text 1 explains larger bricks as evasion of the 1784 duty. Text 2 does not deny that bricks grew, and even allows that the duty may have hurried the change along, but it points to larger bricks before 1784 and outside the duty area, and to clay and kiln as what governed size. That is a judgement that Text 1's account is reasonable as far as it goes but leaves out a cause already operating.

whyWrong.B: Text 2 rests its case on surviving bricks from several counties, so it plainly regards the evidence as available.
whyWrong.C: Text 2 does not dispute the date; it accepts 1784 and argues about what the size change means.
whyWrong.D: Text 2 raises evidence from several counties and does correct Text 1, so it is not endorsing it in every respect.

commonMistakes: Treating any disagreement as flat contradiction; Text 2 explicitly concedes the duty may have accelerated the change.

whyCorrect: The passage names two savings. The clay comes out nearly dry, so it can be pressed straight away instead of being tempered with water and left in the open for weeks. It also carries oil throughout, so once the setting reaches a certain heat the bricks burn from within and need very little more coal. The next sentence calls these two of the heaviest charges on an ordinary yard.

whyWrong.A: Location is never given as a reason; the passage explains the district's share by the properties of the clay.
whyWrong.C: The clay is described as pressed in a machine rather than moulded by hand.
whyWrong.D: Sorting after burning is never mentioned.

tips: For an "according to the text" question, count the reasons the passage actually gives and pick the choice that matches them.

whyCorrect: The passage gives bamboo two practical advantages, that it goes up on a worker's shoulder without the crane and that nylon lashings make a joint anywhere along a pole in seconds. It then sets against that a real limitation: no designed and certified capacity, and fitness judged by experienced eyes rather than by calculation. The main idea has to hold both halves together.

whyWrong.A: Steel tube is described as arriving by lorry, so it is plainly available.
whyWrong.B: The lashings are credited with speed of jointing, not with matching steel's strength, and the text says capacity cannot be certified.
whyWrong.D: No comparison of load capacity between a pole and a tube is made anywhere.

commonMistakes: Ignoring the sentence that opens "Set against that"; a main idea must account for the concession as well as the advantages.

whyCorrect: Hold the tile length fixed and read across. At 265 mm the gauge falls from 100 mm to 90 mm as the lap rises from 65 to 85; at 337 mm it falls from 136 mm to 126 mm for the same change. A smaller gauge means the battens are closer together, so more courses are needed to cover the same slope.

whyWrong.A: This reverses the table; a larger lap gives a smaller gauge, not a larger one.
whyWrong.B: The lap plainly changes the gauge, by 10 mm at each tile length.
whyWrong.C: The longer tile takes the larger gauge, 136 against 100 at 65 mm lap and 126 against 90 at 85 mm.

tips: With two variables in a table, hold one constant and read down the other; comparing rows that differ in both tells you nothing.

whyCorrect: Anand's proposal shifts the failure from the plaster keys to the nails holding the laths. Support therefore has to show the keys intact and the nail fixing gone, which is exactly what choice D reports: keys whole and still hooked over their laths, and enlarged, rust-stained nail holes in the joists. It rules out the standard explanation and confirms his in the same observation.

whyWrong.A: Age at failure is consistent with either explanation, since both keys and nails deteriorate over time.
whyWrong.B: Damp would accelerate rust but also weaken plaster, so it does not separate the two accounts.
whyWrong.C: Fibre in the plaster concerns the strength of the plaster itself and says nothing about the nails.

tips: When two causes are proposed, the strongest finding is the one that shows one mechanism intact while the other has failed.

whyCorrect: Otieno claims the joint profile matters more than the mortar's composition. To test that you have to hold the material constant and vary only the shape, which is what choice A does: identical brick and identical mortar, one weather-struck and one raked, absorbing water at rates differing by a factor of three. The size of the difference under a controlled comparison is what makes it strong support.

whyWrong.B: This varies the mortar rather than the profile, so it supports the rival explanation.
whyWrong.C: The historical frequency of raked joints says nothing about how much water either profile admits.
whyWrong.D: Speed of working is a labour question with no bearing on wetness.

commonMistakes: Accepting evidence that shows one factor matters. The claim is comparative, so the other factor has to be held constant.

whyCorrect: The passage says two courses of slate break the run of pores and that nothing passes them. If damp appears well above that barrier, it cannot have come up from the ground through the pores, so it must have entered by some other route, such as the face of the wall or a leak above.

whyWrong.B: Height is not the issue; the slate stops the rise wherever it sits, and the passage puts it near the foot of the wall.
whyWrong.C: The premise of the sentence is a wall that has the slate in it, so its absence cannot be proved.
whyWrong.D: This contradicts the passage's flat statement that nothing passes the slate.

tips: When a passage says a barrier stops something completely, anything found on the far side has to have arrived another way.

whyCorrect: The passage is explicit that a single fixed pulley gains no force at all, since the pull on the rope equals the load on the hook; it only changes the direction of the pull. So a labourer's ceiling of two bags is set by how hard he can pull, not by anything the wheel can improve.

whyWrong.A: Rope length does not affect the force required; a longer rope simply means more of it to haul.
whyWrong.C: A larger pulley changes nothing about the ratio, which is fixed at one to one for a single fixed pulley.
whyWrong.D: Friction is never mentioned, and the passage attributes the limit to the equality of pull and load.

tips: A single fixed pulley redirects force without multiplying it, so the operator's own strength is the whole of the limit.

whyCorrect: The subject "The burning" governs both verbs: it closes the pores and leaves a surface. Two verbs sharing one subject form a compound predicate, and a compound predicate takes no comma before the conjunction.

whyWrong.A: The comma would be correct only if a second independent clause followed, but "leaves a surface" has no subject of its own.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon requires a complete sentence on each side, and the words after the blank are only a predicate.
whyWrong.D: A full stop leaves "And leaves a surface that a wet cloth will not soak into" as a fragment.

tips: Before putting a comma in front of "and," check whether the words after it have their own subject; if not, leave the comma out.
